tools.name: configure
tools.description: Bring the renderer up: the token its one caller will present, and optionally the domains a journey may navigate to. The runtime keeps every other endpoint at HTTP 503 until this succeeds. Nothing here is written to disk: this service has no volume, and holds the token in memory only.

caller_token.description: The shared secret the calling monitor presents on every render. Attestation tells the caller which build it is talking to; this tells the renderer which caller is talking to it. At least 32 characters.

allowed_domains.description: Comma-separated domains a journey may navigate to, subdomains included. Empty means any, which is appropriate when exactly one caller holds the token and keeps its own allowlist.

tools.name: render
tools.description: Run a scripted journey in a headless browser and report what the page did: per-step outcomes, the document's rendered text, screenshots where the journey asked for them, console errors and failed subresource requests. It reaches no conclusion about availability; the caller decides what the result means, because the caller is the one that has to prove its arithmetic afterwards.

steps.description: Ordered actions: goto, click, fill, press, wait, sleep, text, screenshot, eval.

timeout_ms.description: Budget for the whole journey. Default and maximum 120000.

user_agent.description: How to identify to the watched service.

ocr.description: Also recognise text in each screenshot. Worth it only for words a page draws rather than writes; the document's own text is better and free.

store.tagline: A headless browser as an attested service: it renders a scripted journey and reports what the page did, holding nothing.
store.keywords: headless browser, chromium, screenshots, synthetic monitoring, attestation, ra-tls, confidential computing, tdx
store.description:
A headless browser that runs inside a confidential VM and renders a scripted journey for a caller that has verified its measurement.

IT HOLDS NOTHING
No volume, no vault, no state between calls. Each journey runs in a fresh browser profile that does not survive the process, so one journey cannot see another's session, and a compromised page has nothing to find.

IT DECIDES NOTHING
The renderer reports what happened: which step failed and why, the document's rendered text, screenshots where they were asked for, console errors, and the subresources that failed to load. It draws no conclusion about whether a service is up. That belongs to the caller, which has to be able to prove its arithmetic later.

WHY IT IS SEPARATE
A monitoring service that can be trusted with a real account should not also be parsing whatever a watched page returns. Splitting the browser into its own enclave, with its own measurement, keeps the page away from the credentials and the availability record.
